tweets.text:
The best traders are very fluid

You could have had an idea yesterday, thats no longer valid today or whatever time frame. But ultimately, you aren't married to any idea or position. Whether you are trading eth, or wheat futures. All that matters is your pnl. They are really just tickers to trade with changing narratives, rotations, and liquidity. Sometimes people get on a trend late and still make more than someone who was early. People are wrong all the time, but the best learn to correct it quick and admit that. More often than not marrying a ticker comes with many big costs whether emotional, or financially. 

All that matters is what you make, and keep, and that we get paid for the risk we take. See so many people crap on people who had an idea one week, and then the opposite week their opinion changed as new information came in. That's exactly how you are suppose to be. fluid

tweets.text:
i think the new capabilities are going to really make a dent in places where the economics previously just didn’t make sense

for example, people paying attention to VR know we’re already seeing an unexpected renaissance there. it previously never made sense to make a true AAA game in VR because there aren’t enough people who own headsets for you to possibly return the investment, even if the game is phenomenal

but now people can take existing PC games, mod them with claude in one weekend to play absolutely fantastic in VR, and we’re getting experiences that are absolutely mind blowing in the last few weeks

you could say this “kills” the commercial VR gaming industry but.. it was already dead!

but for major video games, i actually am not convinced it changes much. most “live service” games were already slop and rejected by the market before ai. this trend will continue

but are you telling me that if half life 3 is released tomorrow you’re not going to buy it, because you can make your own threejs games? that’s absurd. where there’s a brand and a story that people care about, they’ll pay for the experience. where there isn’t, they won’t. and this was already the case

📊 DAILY METALS PULSE — WEEKLY CLOSE
📅 Friday, 2 October 2026

Q4 opens with a difficult mix: weaker U.S. hiring eased fears of another Fed hike, but elevated bond yields and a stronger dollar over the week kept metals under pressure.

☢️ URANIUM
TradeTech reports utilities seeking fuel for deliveries from 2027 into the late 2030s. Long-term contracting remains the signal I’m watching: securing reactor fuel extends well beyond this week’s market mood.

🥈 SILVER
A tough week, with monetary headwinds weighing alongside gold. The Silver Institute forecasts a sixth consecutive annual supply deficit in 2026. That supports my longer-term conviction, although deficits alone cannot prevent sharp corrections.

🥉 COPPER
Growth worries meet supply concerns. Reuters reports China wants copper supply commitments before approving the Anglo–Teck merger. To me, that underlines how strategically important reliable access to copper has become.

🥇 GOLD
Friday’s initial rally after the jobs report faded. High yields remain a hurdle, while softer hiring complicates the Fed’s fight against inflation.

My take: I remain constructive on the longer-term metals story. Next week, I’m watching the dollar, bond yields and whether physical supply concerns translate into stronger sentiment for miners.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the Daily Metals Pulse.

Chamath: 3 Things Every Company Needs in the Age of Super Intelligence

1) End-to-End Traceability

2) Policy-to-Risk Mapping

3) Auditable Evidence

@Chamath:

“There's really three things that you're going to need in an age of super intelligence so that boards are protected, CEOs have visibility, and all of the other compliance infrastructure and governance infrastructure of a company like D&O Insurance and all these other things are kept in place, which is end-to-end traceability, right?

Which is to say, when you deploy super intelligence, you need to know what's going on. You need to map it to the policies so that you understand what the risks are. All companies have standard operating procedures, but you need to know exactly when you're deploying super intelligence, how that builds on top of your standard operating procedure, so you need to map policies to risk.

And then the third is you need to have auditable evidence, which is your way of showing all of your downstream ecosystem, ‘Here's what I've done.’

So if anybody taps you on the shoulder, whether it's a lawyer, whether it's an auditor, whether it's a regulator, whether it's in a lawsuit, whether it's a customer, ‘Hey, how did this happen?’ You can present something. So these are, like, very practical, sane things, and you have this solution where the alternative was to hit the pause on trillions of dollars of GDP so that we could sort this out in a multinational body.

The alternative was crazy, so I think what happened was historic and important.”

I love this chart.

In 1993 the German electricity companies said renewables could never supply more than 4% of the country's power... that was the ceiling. Last year they supplied 55.9%. Fourteen times the ceiling.

It's the psychology of incumbents meeting exponential change. They extrapolate from the flat part of the curve, and the ceiling turns out to be a speed bump. Same story in EVs, in crypto, in AI...

Impossible, then inevitable.
